To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the loss of DNA mismatch-repair (MMR) increases the ability of the chemotherapeutic agent cisplatin to induce resistance to the molecular target drugs topotecan and paclitaxis and to the nucleoside analog gemcitabine.

the loss of mismatch repair (MM) increases the ability of the chemotherapeutic drug cisplatin (CDDP) to generate variants resistant in vitro to the topoisomerase I inhibitors topotecan and irinotecan, to the ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor gemcitabine (2',2'-difluorodeoxycytidine, dFdC), and possibly to paclitaxe (Pac).
(a) Loss of MMR increases sensitivity to cisplatin-induced mutagenesis and (b) loss of MMR causes an increased rate of spontaneous mutagenesis.

the loss of mismatch repair increases the frequency of spontaneous and drug-induced mutations in both coding (topotecan and gemcicitabine) and non-coding (paclitaxel) sequences.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the loss of mismatch repair in human tumor cells increases their resistance to cisplatin, which is a major component of many chemotherapeutic regimens, and that this loss also increases the ability of these cells to generate resistant variants to other drugs with different mechanisms of action, which may be an additional mechanism by which loss of MMR contributes to chemoresistance.
loss of MMR causes a marked increase in the frequency of variants that are resistant to the single molecular target drugs tested, but that the effect is drug specific.
MMR-deficient tumors will develop resistance to chemotherapy more rapidly than MMR-proficient tumors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MMR-deficient tumors may be more sensitive to the development of drug resistance than MMR-proficient tumors.
MMR-deficient cells are more resistant to the mutagenesis of cisplatin and more likely to generate resistant variants after exposure to the drug.
